name: Gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina

reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Scriver's Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive chorioretinal dystrophy caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme ornithine aminotransferase (OAT gene), leading to hyperornithinaemia
Presents in childhood or early adult life with progressive night blindness (nyctalopia) and constricting peripheral visual fields
Fundus shows sharply demarcated, scalloped (gyrate) circular patches of chorioretinal atrophy in the mid-periphery that coalesce and extend centrally over time
Plasma ornithine concentration is markedly elevated, providing a key biochemical clue that distinguishes it from other retinal dystrophies
High myopia and posterior subcapsular cataract are common associated ocular features
The electroretinogram becomes progressively reduced and eventually extinguished as the disease advances
An arginine-restricted diet to lower plasma ornithine, sometimes with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation in responsive subtypes, may slow retinal degeneration
reference.pathophysiology: Gyrate atrophy is caused by biallelic mutations in the OAT gene encoding ornithine aminotransferase, a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that converts ornithine to glutamate semialdehyde. Enzyme deficiency causes ornithine to accumulate in plasma and tissues. Chronically raised ornithine is thought to be toxic to the retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris, producing progressive atrophy of the choroid and outer retina. The metabolic block also disturbs the urea cycle and creatine synthesis pathways. The characteristic well-circumscribed peripheral chorioretinal lesions enlarge and merge, ultimately encroaching on the macula and destroying central vision.
additionalInvestigations: Fasting plasma amino acid analysis demonstrating markedly elevated ornithine
Electroretinography showing progressive rod and cone dysfunction
Optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence to map areas of atrophy
Visual field testing documenting peripheral constriction
Assay of ornithine aminotransferase activity in fibroblasts and molecular OAT gene testing
Assessment of pyridoxine responsiveness of plasma ornithine
redFlags: Rapidly constricting visual fields with impending loss of central fixation
Development of dense cataract compounding retinal visual loss
Poor dietary adherence with persistently high plasma ornithine accelerating degeneration
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressive, and most patients experience severe visual impairment or blindness by middle age; dietary control of ornithine and pyridoxine supplementation in responsive individuals may slow but not fully arrest the decline.
pitfalls: Confusing the fundus appearance with choroideremia or high myopia and missing the treatable metabolic cause
Failing to check plasma ornithine in a young patient with unexplained progressive chorioretinal atrophy
Assuming all patients respond to pyridoxine when only a subset are responsive
Neglecting long-term dietary monitoring and family genetic counselling
references: Scriver's The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
